title: Algebra and Functions
lines: USAT includes about 4 questions on algebra and functions. They test whether you can simplify and factorise expressions, handle indices (powers), work with function notation, and spot patterns in sequences. The level is SSC to HSSC mathematics; every question is designed to be done by hand in about a minute.
## Indices
| Rule | Example
| aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ | x³ × x⁴ = x⁷
| aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ | x⁸ ÷ x² = x⁶
| (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ | (x²)⁵ = x¹⁰
| a to the power m/n = (nth root of a) to the power m | 27 to the power 2/3 = 3² = 9
- To solve an index equation, write both sides as powers of the same base: 4 to the power x = 32 becomes 2 to the power 2x = 2⁵, so x = 5/2.
## Expanding and factorising
- (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² and (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²
- a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b). It also makes arithmetic easy: 51² − 49² = 2 × 100 = 200.
- a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²) and a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²)
- For x² + bx + c, find two numbers with product c and sum b. For ax² + bx + c, find two numbers with product ac and sum b, then split the middle term.
- Factor theorem: (x − k) is a factor of p(x) exactly when p(k) = 0. The remainder when p(x) is divided by (x − k) is p(k).
- Cancel only factors, never terms: (x² − 9)/(x + 3) = x − 3, but (x² + 9)/x² is not 9.
## Functions
A function f takes an input x and gives exactly one output f(x). To find f(3), replace every x by 3, using brackets for negatives.
- Composition: f(g(x)) means do g first, then f. In general f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) are different.
- Domain: the inputs allowed. Exclude values that make a denominator zero, and values that make the number under a square root negative.
- Range: the outputs produced. x² is never negative, so x² − 3 has range y ≥ −3.
- Inverse of a linear function: write y = f(x), make x the subject, then swap x and y. f⁻¹(a) is the input that gives output a, so f⁻¹(a) = b exactly when f(b) = a.
## Sequences
- Arithmetic (common difference d): nth term = a + (n − 1)d; sum of n terms = n/2 × [2a + (n − 1)d], or n × (first + last)/2.
- Geometric (common ratio r): nth term = a × r to the power (n − 1); sum of n terms = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1).
- If neither fits, look at the differences between terms: 3, 5, 9, 15, 23 has differences 2, 4, 6, 8.
## Worked examples
> If f(x) = 3x + 2 and g(x) = x², find f(g(−2)) and g(f(−2)).
> f(−2) = −4, so g(f(−2)) = (−4)² = 16. The order matters.
> Find f⁻¹(x) when f(x) = (2x − 1)/5.
> Check with a number: f(3) = 1, and f⁻¹(1) = 6/2 = 3.
> The 4th term of an arithmetic sequence is 17 and the 9th term is 37. Find the first term.
> Five steps of d take 17 to 37, so 5d = 20 and d = 4. Then a = 17 − 3 × 4 = 5.
! f⁻¹(x) is not 1/f(x). The inverse undoes the function; the reciprocal just turns the output upside down.
! (a + b)² is not a² + b². The middle term 2ab is the most commonly forgotten piece in USAT algebra.
! A negative index gives a reciprocal, not a negative number: 2⁻² = 1/4.
## Quick check
- Can you evaluate 16 to the power 3/4 in your head? (It is 8.)
- Can you factorise x² − x − 12 in under ten seconds?
- Do you always do the inside function first in f(g(x))?
- Can you tell an arithmetic sequence from a geometric one at a glance?
